body_html:
Some ideas look obvious in hindsight. This one still isn’t.

It’s a small name in financials trading at a lower P/E than peers even though its ROE is consistently higher. The only metric that looks “expensive” is P/B, and that’s well-deserved given the its asset quality and durability.

The market shrugs because insiders hold about half the shares, liquidity is thin, and the market cap sits under $500 million. Coverage is light.

I see 50% upside over the next 1–2 years as earnings compound and valuation normalizes. Over five years, this stock could easily double.

If you want to know the name, upgrade to paid ($130 per year). One good stock idea can cover that fee and then some.

Trade alert:

  • Buy BSVN

Table of Contents:

  • TLDR

  • Company History & Evolution

  • Industry Landscape, Growth Levers & Outlook

  • Competitors and Bank7’s Edge

  • Management Quality & Capital Allocation

  • Financials

  • Valuation: What’s Bank7 Worth?

  • Risks and the Bear Case

  • Other Angles: Long-Term Thesis Support

  • Verdict: A Big “Buy” on This Small Bank

TLDR

I believe Bank7 Corp. (BSVN) is a gem among community banks. It’s a lean, high-performing bank with exceptional profitability and fortress-like balance sheet quality. Bank7 consistently earns over double the returns of typical banks with net interest margins around 5% vs. 3% for peers, and ROA near 2.3% vs. 1% peers.

It operates in business-friendly markets (Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas) and keeps costs ultra-low (efficiency ratio sub-40% vs. 64% peer median). Despite these strengths, the stock trades at just 9x earnings, a discount to similar banks. With robust loan growth, a rock-solid capital base, and insiders who’ve built the bank over decades, Bank7 offers an attractive mix of growth and value.

That is why I chose BSVN as November’s stock pick as I see upside as the bank’s earnings compound (15% yearly EPS growth assumed) and the market recognizes its superior performance. In short, Bank7 is a small bank with a big edge and a buy in my book.

Company History & Evolution

Bank7’s story begins in a small Oklahoma town over a century ago. The bank traces its roots to First National Bank of Medford, chartered in 1901. In the mid-2000s, current management saw an opportunity to revitalize and expand this sleepy community bank. Brad Haines and his family acquired the institution in 2004, moved the headquarters to Oklahoma City in 2005, and rebranded it as “Bank7.” The name signals a fresh start (and a nod to lucky number seven), but the bank kept its community focus.

Since then, Bank7 has evolved from one rural branch into a multi-state regional bank. Today it operates 12 locations across Oklahoma, the Dallas/Fort Worth metroplex in Texas, and Kansas. These are pro-growth markets: think energy, agriculture, and booming DFW suburbs. The bank still specializes in serving local business owners and entrepreneurs, much like a friendly hometown bank, but with the financial firepower to handle bigger deals.

Management emphasizes “fast, consistent and well-designed” loan and deposit products tailored to small business needs. In plain English, they pride themselves on quick decisions and custom solutions; a nimble approach that big banks often lack.

Bank7’s growth has been mostly organic (opening branches in promising locations), though they remain open to strategic acquisitions. The Haines family and insiders retain significant ownership, aligning management with shareholders. After years of private ownership, Bank7 Corp. went public in 2018, giving it access to capital and a broader investor base. Since the IPO, the bank has steadily compounded its balance sheet and earnings, sticking to what it does best: traditional community banking with an entrepreneurial twist.

Throughout its evolution, one thing stayed constant: conservative banking practices. Bank7 avoided flashy fintech fads or risky trading bets. It’s essentially a traditional bank, gathering local deposits and making loans, but it does so extraordinarily well. This focus has created a small but mighty franchise that’s now punching above its weight in terms of profitability and growth.

How Bank7 Makes Money

Bank7 makes money the old-fashioned way for a bank: taking in deposits and lending them out, while keeping costs low.

  • Deposits: Local customers (businesses and individuals) park their money at Bank7, and the bank pays them interest. Bank7 has grown its deposit base to about $1.64 billion as of Q3 2025. A large portion of these deposits are low-cost non-interest-bearing and transaction accounts, meaning Bank7 isn’t overpaying for funds. In fact, only 24.6% of deposits are uninsured (above FDIC limits), which is comfortably low. This lowers risk, because it means most depositors are within insurance limits and less likely to flee in a panic, a key lesson from recent bank scares.

  • Loans: Bank7 primarily lends to businesses. As of Q3 2025, loans were about $1.51 billion, up from $1.38B a year prior. These loans are well-diversified across commercial industries and real estate. The largest segment is commercial & industrial (C&I) loans (26% of the portfolio). These might fund a local manufacturer or service company. Next are loans for hospitality (hotels) at 19%, and other commercial real estate like non-owner-occupied properties, 1-4 family rental properties, and construction loans. Importantly, Bank7 has minimal exposure to risky office real estate as only about 5% of the loan book involves office buildings. That’s a relief given high office vacancy rates these days. In short, Bank7 lends across various sectors but avoids over-concentration in any single troubled area.

  • Interest Income: By lending money out, the bank earns interest from borrowers. Bank7’s loan yields have been quite high, north of 7% recently. Many loans are tied to variable rates (about 79% of loans are variable-rate), which means as interest rates rose over the past couple years, Bank7’s loan interest income also climbed. The bank also earns a smaller portion of interest from a modest securities portfolio (they keep a small amount in bonds) and cash reserves. Net interest income (interest earned minus interest paid to depositors) is the lifeblood of Bank7’s earnings. In Q3 2025, net interest income was $22.3 million, up from $21.2M in Q3 2024 thanks to loan growth and a still-strong net interest margin.

  • Fees & Other Income: Like most banks, Bank7 also earns some non-interest income (fees). This includes things like service charges, mortgage banking income, etc. However, it’s a relatively small piece of the pie. For example, in Q3 2025, non-interest income was about $2.2 million, actually down from the prior year. Bank7 isn’t leaning on tricky trading income or complex derivatives and it’s mainly sticking to core banking revenues.

  • Keeping Costs Low: One big way Bank7 makes more profit is by spending far less than peers. It has an efficiency ratio under 40%, which is remarkably low. (Efficiency ratio = non-interest expenses / revenue, so lower means the bank is more efficient). The peer median is around 64% meaning many banks spend 60% as much of each revenue dollar on overhead than Bank7 does. Bank7 achieves this by running lean operations. They have only 12 branches and a relatively small staff (124 FTEs) focused on high-value relationships. Management highlights having “fewer but high-quality bankers” and a tight process that avoids waste.

In summary, Bank7’s money-making formula is highly profitable community banking. Gather local deposits (mostly insured, low-cost) → make diverse loans with healthy yields → control expenses fiercely → and repeat. This straightforward model has produced exceptional margins for Bank7, as we’ll see when comparing to industry peers.

Industry Landscape, Growth Levers & Outlook

Bank7 operates in the U.S. regional banking industry, which in recent years has seen its share of challenges and opportunities.

Rising then Falling Rates

Over 2022-2023, the Federal Reserve hiked interest rates at the fastest clip in decades.

This was a boon for banks’ loan yields, but also raised their deposit costs. Banks like Bank7 benefited from higher interest income, although they had to start paying up to keep depositors. By late 2024 and into 2025, interest rates stabilized at high levels, and now the outlook is for potential rate cuts as inflation cools. A declining rate environment is on the horizon going into 2026. What does this mean for Bank7? In the short run, Bank7 is actually in a sweet spot: about 79% of its loans are variable-rate but many have interest rate floors.

This means even if rates tick down, the loan rates won’t drop below certain minimums, protecting interest income. Meanwhile, a lot of its deposits have no floors so Bank7 can lower the rates it pays on deposits immediately as market rates fall. Management believes this positions them well for initial rate declines.

However, longer-term if rates fall substantially, virtually all banks (including Bank7) will see margins compress. In Bank7’s case, a whopping 95% of its loans reprice or mature within 5 years. So over a couple of years, loan yields will catch down to the new lower rates. In other words, Bank7 can fend off margin pressure for a little while (thanks to loan floors and sticky deposit costs), but over a multi-year period, lower rates will mean lower net interest margin. The good news is every bank faces this, and Bank7’s superior efficiency should help it handle a margin squeeze better than most peers.

Banking Turbulence & Depositor Behavior

2023 was a wild year for banks, with a few high-profile bank failures (Silicon Valley Bank, etc.) causing jitters about uninsured deposits. Many regional banks saw deposit outflows as customers moved money to the perceived safety of big banks or higher-yield instruments.

Bank7 was not immune to this industry trend. Its deposits actually dipped from $1.59B at the end of 2023 to $1.52B at end of 2024. This was a 5% drop, likely reflecting some customers shopping for higher rates or diversifying funds amid the turmoil. Crucially, Bank7’s deposit base rebounded to $1.55B in Q1 2025 and continued growing to $1.64B by Q3 2025.

So the bank managed to regain and grow deposits after the blip, suggesting that its customers value the relationship and returned once dust settled. With 24% uninsured deposits (or under 19% if you exclude insider/collateralized accounts), Bank7 has one of the lowest risk profiles in terms of fickle big depositors. This bodes well in an industry where deposit stability is now a key focus.

Economic Conditions & Loan Growth

Bank7’s markets (Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas) are heavily influenced by energy, agriculture, and general commercial activity. In 2023-2024, rising interest rates cooled off some loan demand industry-wide. Yet Bank7 still grew loans by about 3% in 2024 and accelerated in 2025 (loans up ~9% y/y by Q3 2025).

A growth lever here is Bank7’s reputation for quick, tailored lending. They attract borrowers who need fast decisions or are overlooked by larger banks. As long as the regional economy remains reasonably healthy, Bank7 expects high-single-digit loan growth going forward. Management has a robust pipeline of deals, though they noted some competition is easing loan yields a bit (new loans coming in around 7.0–7.25% yield versus hopes of 7.4%).

Looking ahead now that the Fed has begun cutting rates, there is a renewed opportunity for borrowing to pick up as businesses refinancing or expanding could drive demand. Bank7 Corp. is positioned well: it has strong liquidity and capital, so it can act when others pull back. Many banks remain cautious or are shrinking certain portfolios due to capital constraints; Bank7’s zero holding-company debt and healthy equity cushion give it the freedom to be opportunistic in lending while others sit on the sidelines.

Regulation and Capital

The banking industry is facing potentially tighter regulation post-2023’s mini-crisis, especially for banks in the +$100B range. For a tiny bank like Bank7 ( <$2B assets), regulatory changes are less onerous, but still something to watch (e.g. increased FDIC insurance costs spread across all banks). Bank7 already operates with capital ratios far above required minimums.

Its CET1 (Common Equity Tier 1) ratio is 14.2%, which is double the regulatory “well-capitalized” benchmark of 6.5%. In practical terms, Bank7 has a thick equity cushion to absorb losses or support growth. This high capital and no holding-company debt gives regulators comfort and provides flexibility for the bank to increase dividends or share buybacks (or do acquisitions) in the future. Industry-wide, many banks are constrained by capital, but Bank7 shines here as a well-capitalized outlier.

Technology and Competition

Even as a smaller bank, Bank7 has to compete with megabanks (Chase, BofA etc.) and fintechs that woo customers with digital convenience. Bank7’s approach is to combine enough technology (online banking, mobile apps… they have all the standard digital services) with the high-touch service of a community bank.

This strategy seems to work in their niche as they aren’t trying to be everything to everyone nationwide, but rather compete on relationship lending and local decision-making. In its markets, plenty of customers still prefer a banker they can call directly. Bank7 likely won’t lead the industry in tech, but it doesn’t appear to be behind either. The low efficiency ratio also implies they leverage tech smartly to keep headcount lean.

Outlook

Overall, the banking industry is in a late-cycle phase where margins may tighten as rates fall and loan growth could moderate if a recession hits. However, Bank7’s outlook remains solid because it has multiple levers: it can gain market share from weaker competitors, maintain profitability with low costs, and it has room to keep growing loans organically.

Even if net interest margin compresses a bit from the current 5%, Bank7 could offset some of that by growing volume (more loans) and by reducing deposit costs. The bank’s asset quality and conservative underwriting also mean it’s less likely to be derailed by credit problems if the economy softens. In fact, credit trends have been improving for Bank7 (non-performing assets have decreased over the past year), unlike some banks seeing rising delinquencies.

Competitors and Bank7’s Edge

Bank7 competes with a broad range of other banks, from local community banks to regional players in its markets. But rather than name every competitor, let’s focus on how Bank7 stacks up in key metrics versus peers. This is where Bank7’s “secret sauce” becomes clear as its performance metrics are among the best in the nation for banks of similar size.

I’ll compare Bank7 to a peer group of small US banks (assets $500M–$5B) as well as note specific peers used in recent analysis (like Civista Bancshares, Carter Bankshares, etc.).

Net Interest Margin (NIM)

This measures the bank’s lending spread (essentially interest yield on assets minus interest cost on liabilities). Bank7’s NIM is exceptionally high. In 2024, BSVN’s NIM was 5.11% vs 3.13% for the peer median. As of Q2 2025 it was around 4.96% for Bank7, versus 3.45% median peer.

This means Bank7 earns about 1.5 percentage points more on each dollar of assets than the average small bank, a huge edge.

How? It’s partly due to the high loan yields in Bank7’s niche (many commercial loans at variable rates) and low-cost deposits. Also, Bank7 doesn’t carry a lot of low-yield investments. Its securities portfolio is tiny (only $60M), so most assets are in higher-yielding loans.

Peers often hold more bonds which dragged their NIM down when rates rose (since many bonds are fixed rate and lost value). Bank7 avoided that trap by keeping securities minimal and even cutting them from $169M in 2023 to $60M in 2024. A move that freed up funds for loans.

Return on Assets (ROA)

This tells how efficiently the bank turns assets into profit. Bank7’s ROA for the recent quarter was about 2.3–2.5%, which is outstanding (anything above 1% is considered good in banking). Peers are around 1% or less ROA typically. For instance, in Q2 2025 small-bank peers had a median ROA (net income as % of assets) of about 1.00%, while Bank7 posted 2.47%.

This means Bank7 generates roughly $2.47 of profit for every $100 of assets vs. $1.00 for the average peer. That’s like 2.5x more efficient at squeezing profit from its balance sheet.

Return on Equity (ROE)

Bank7’s equity returns aren’t a one-off. They’ve been higher than peers for years.

The bank’s return on average tangible common equity (ROATCE) averages 21.4% over five years. Recent prints are 20.7% in Q2 2025 and 19.1% in Q3 2025.

The peer median sat around 11.4% in Q2 2025. That gap has been consistent since 2021.

High ROATCE reflects the same story you see in the income statement: net income to average assets at 2.47% vs 1.00% for peers in Q2 2025. High, repeatable returns grow book value and give management room to raise dividends or buy back stock without starving growth.

Efficiency Ratio

We touched on this, but to reiterate, Bank7’s efficiency ratio is under 40%, whereas peers are 64%.

A lower number means it spends less to earn a dollar of revenue. Bank7 is literally +60% more efficient than peer banks. Competitors must either accept lower profits or try to cut costs to catch up which not easy without disrupting service. Bank7’s lean model (few branches, fewer employees per asset) is a structural advantage that isn’t quickly replicable by an inefficient competitor.

Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) Capital

Bank7’s CET1 is about 14.2% of risk-weighted assets.

Many peers of similar size run CET1 in the 10–12% range. For example, a peer like Civista (CIVB) was around 11.6% CET1 last I checked, and Carter Bankshares (CARE) 10.7%.

Higher CET1 means Bank7 has a larger safety net and more capacity to grow assets or absorb losses. It’s significantly “over-capitalized” relative to minimum requirements (well-cap threshold is 6.5%).

While excess capital can drag ROE a bit, Bank7 has managed high ROEs even with the strong capital. This capital strength gives it an edge in trustworthiness and potential to capitalize on opportunities. During industry stress, a bank like Bank7 with ample capital and no debt can be a safe harbor or even acquire assets from weaker rivals.

Price-to-Earnings (P/E) Ratio

Despite better performance, Bank7’s stock is cheaper than many peers on earnings.

At around $41 per share and roughly $4.50 trailing twelve-month EPS, BSVN trades near 9x TTM earnings. Peers often trade between 10–12× earnings for banks with decent growth.

So we are not paying a premium for this high-quality name. If anything, it’s at a discount. This could be due to its small-cap nature ($390M market cap) or lower liquidity of the stock. But it suggests upside if the market re-rates Bank7 to a fairer multiple given its superior metrics. (More on valuation soon.)

Price-to-Book (P/B) Ratio

One area where Bank7 looks expensive is on book value.

It trades above 1.6x book value, whereas many peers are closer to 1.0–1.3x. This is the flip side of high ROE and high earnings. Its book value has grown but the market also values those earnings power.

I view the high P/B as justified by Bank7’s outlier profitability. Essentially, investors are willing to pay more than a dollar for a dollar of Bank7’s net assets because those assets produce much more income. Peers with mediocre ROEs trade at low P/B for a reason (their earnings don’t cover their cost of equity well).

So Bank7’s edge is that it earns enough to warrant a premium P/B. That said, if Bank7 stumbled and earnings fell, a high P/B could become a risk factor for the stock price. But given current performance, the premium P/B is a sign of a quality franchise.

In summary, Bank7’s edge over competitors is quantitatively clear: higher margins, higher returns, and a fortress balance sheet. They’ve carved out a niche where they run much leaner and more profitable than typical banks their size.

It’s worth noting competitors might try to emulate some of Bank7’s tactics, but structural advantages (like Bank7’s specific market focus, long-term client relationships, and insider ownership driving efficiency) aren’t easily copied overnight. Many banks simply can’t get their NIM above 5% without taking on big risks, nor can they slash their efficiency to 38% without major upheaval. Bank7 has been built from the ground up with this culture of efficiency and prudent risk-taking.

As a result, when comparing Bank7 to other community banks, Bank7 stands out as one of the top performers on nearly every key metric. This fundamental edge is why I’m comfortable picking it as a top idea; it’s not just a value play, it’s an operationally superior bank.

Management Quality & Capital Allocation

A bank is only as good as its management, especially a smaller bank that relies on lending and cost discipline. In Bank7’s case, management quality is a strong asset. The Haines family (led by CEO Thomas L. Travis, and Chairman Brad Haines) has been at the helm through the bank’s modern history.

They have a significant ownership stake, aligning their interests with shareholders. They want the stock to do well over the long term, not just meet the next quarter’s targets.

Key aspects of management’s prowess:

Conservative Underwriting

Bank7’s leadership has instilled tight credit standards.

Evidence? The bank had minimal trouble loans even during tough times. Non-performing assets (loans that aren’t being paid on time) were just 0.28% of total assets in Q3 2025.

That’s extremely low and down from 0.43% at end of 2024 and way down from 1.64% in 2023.

Management successfully de-risked the portfolio, reducing exposure to historically volatile sectors like energy. They saw that energy loans were riskier, so over recent years they trimmed energy loan exposure and grew in other areas.

This shows foresight.

They also limited office commercial real estate exposure when everyone knows offices are struggling keeping it under 10% of loans. These decisions reflect a prudent approach to risk.

Focus on Asset Quality

The phrase “asset quality is top-notch” keeps coming up. That comes from management’s constant attention to loan performance. They don’t chase every high-yield loan; they’d rather have slightly lower yield if it means a safer loan.

The result is industry-leading ROA without outsized credit risk. Also, Bank7 carries immaterial goodwill ($11M or 0.6% of assets) and no intangible assets, in other words, it hasn’t overpaid for acquisitions.

Its tangible common equity is solid. Management’s discipline in not doing pricey mergers means shareholders’ equity is real and solid.

Operational Efficiency Culture

The CEO and team have clearly fostered a culture of efficiency. A bank doesn’t hit a sub-40 efficiency ratio by accident. Management has kept branch count low and probably leverages technology and cross-training of staff.

They mention having high-quality bankers and a strict process, which suggests they hire top talent and give them tools to be extremely productive. They also avoid the empire-building mentality that plagues some banks (opening lots of branches or hiring excess staff just to show growth). This lean operating style comes from the top.

Capital Allocation & Shareholder Returns

Bank7’s management has been smart in deploying capital. They retained earnings to grow the bank when needed (hence the strong capital ratios), but they haven’t sat on lazy capital either.

They pay a regular dividend (currently yielding around 2.4%. Not huge, but a nice steady payout).

The dividend payout ratio is low (15.65% of earnings), implying they reinvest most profits into growth, which makes sense given they can earn +20% ROE by growing the loan book.

This shows a willingness to return capital that’s truly excess. They have done some share buybacks historically, but not aggressively likely because the stock already trades above book, so buybacks, while still accretive to EPS, are used judiciously.

Overall, management balances between fueling growth and rewarding shareholders.

Transparency and Execution

Management’s communications (earnings calls, investor presentations) indicate a transparent, “no-nonsense” style. They set achievable targets and hit them. For instance, after Q2 2025’s strong results, management confidently upgraded the outlook and then delivered again in Q3.

They don’t sugarcoat challenges either; they openly flagged that new loan yields were coming in a bit lower and deposit competition was stiff. This candor is good; it means they manage expectations well. Their execution track record is evident in the metrics…consistently high performance each quarter.

Insider Ownership

The Haines family controls a big piece of the company. Between the trusts tied to William Bradford Haines (18.8%), Lisa K. Haines (15.2%), and Julee S. Lawrence (15.1%), insiders together hold close to half of all outstanding shares. That’s rare in banking. It means management’s fortunes move with shareholders, not apart from them.

This high insider ownership is a double-edged sword (low float can make the stock less liquid), but it’s largely positive for long-term holders. It implies management will run the bank conservatively and for long-term value because it’s their money on the line too. There’s no incentive to take wild risks that could blow up the bank.

Community Reputation

While harder to quantify, Bank7’s leadership being local and focused on community relationships likely gives them a reputation advantage. They’ve been banking many clients for years, so there’s trust that management will stick with them through cycles (and vice versa). Competitors often lose ground if they rotate executives or if their decision-making is out-of-state; Bank7 scores points by being stable and local at the top.

Financials

Asset Growth

Since 2016, Bank7 has quietly compounded its balance sheet. Assets grew from about $614 million in 2016 to $1.74 billion at the end of 2024, a 13.9% CAGR.

That’s almost tripling assets in less than a decade. Growth came from steady deposit inflows and disciplined loan expansion, not from big acquisitions. For a community bank, expanding at that rate organically speaks to a strong brand, tight cost control, and deep relationships with local business owners.

Loan & Deposit Trends

Since 2020, Bank7’s loan book has compounded at 13.6% annually, reaching $1.54 billion by Q3 2025.

Growth was broad-based. The mix shows how management stayed disciplined, expanding without stretching credit risk.

Deposits kept pace, rising from $905 million in 2020 to $1.64 billion in Q3 2025, a 13.4% CAGR.

Importantly, non-interest-bearing deposits remain around 21% of the base, reflecting sticky customer relationships. After trimming high-cost deposits in 2024 to defend margins, Bank7 resumed healthy inflows through 2025. The growth has been steady, self-funded, and built on core client trust rather than promotional rate chasing.

Income and Margins

From 2020 to 2024, net interest income nearly doubled, rising from $47.2 million to $86.2 million. That’s a four-year gain of about 90%, powered by a larger loan book and steady margin control.

Over the same period, average earning assets expanded from $941 million to $1.68 billion, showing that Bank7’s growth was not just rate-driven and it came from more productive lending.

The net interest margin (NIM) held impressively steady through rate cycles, moving from 5.01% in 2020 to 5.11% in 2024. Even excluding loan fee income, the margin barely budged from 4.48% to 4.75%, which is remarkable consistency during a volatile rate environment.

The takeaway is clear: Bank7 didn’t chase volume or sacrifice spreads to grow. It priced loans smartly, managed deposit costs with discipline, and kept earning power intact through changing macro cycles.

Earnings

Put it together, and net income jumped from $9.6M in 2013 to $45.7M in 2024. That’s a 4.8x leap (+15% CAGR), reflecting both the release of loan loss provisions and true earnings growth.

Diluted EPS compounded a bit faster at 16% due to modest share buybacks. Diluted EPS grew from $1 in 2023 to $4.75 per share.

ROA for 2024 clocked in around 1.68% (peer median ~0.85%), and ROE hit 18.6% (or 22% on tangible equity). These figures put Bank7 in the top echelon of banks nationwide for profitability.

Credit Quality

In 2024, even as many feared credit issues from rapid rate hikes, Bank7’s asset quality improved. Non-performing assets were only 0.43% of assets at end of 2024, down from a higher level in 2023 (which had that big provision). The 2023 provision now looks like conservative buffer-building, since actual problem loans remained low by end of 2024. Essentially, management “front-loaded” credit costs in 2023 out of caution, and in 2024 the bank reaped the rewards of having a clean loan book.

Capital & Dividends

By 2024, Bank7’s equity-to-assets ratio was around 12.3% (healthy and up from under 10% in 2023, partly thanks to retained earnings swelling equity). CET1 14%.

The bank initiated a modest dividend in 2019 and maintained it as earnings grew; due to the earnings spike, the payout ratio dropped further (meaning they retained most profits to support growth).

Book value per share compounded 16.7% since 2019 due to the high ROE and low payout.

Share Beating The Tide: Stock Picks That Outperform

Valuation: What’s Bank7 Worth?

I approach valuation primarily on a P/E basis, since Bank7’s earnings power is strong and growing. We will also sanity-check with P/B.

Current Valuation: At around $41 per share, Bank7 trades roughly at:

  • 9.1x 2025 full-year earnings (assuming $4.50 EPS for 2025).

  • 1.6x book value.

As I showed earlier, compared to peers, a 9x P/E is a bargain. Banks with similar performance (ROE near 20%, solid growth) would typically fetch low double-digit P/Es at least. Bank7, being one of the strongest, arguably deserves to be at the top end of bank valuations.

Fair P/E Multiple: I conservatively estimate a fair P/E for Bank7 is around 11–12x forward earnings. Why not higher? Historically, small banks often top out around that range unless they’re in a takeover situation. Also, Bank7’s high P/B suggests some valuation premium is already in the stock (investors recognize quality). But given its growth prospects, an argument could be made for >12x. Let’s stay grounded with 11–12x as a target multiple that the stock could reasonably achieve as more investors notice its performance.

Earnings Growth: I assume EPS can grow at a compound annual rate of 15% for the next few years. As I demonstrated earlier in this article, this isn’t pulled from thin air as it’s roughly in line with Bank7’s trajectory. With the expansion into Texas markets and their efficiency, mid-teens growth is attainable. Specifically, growth will come from:

  • Loan growth (high-single digits),

  • Improved funding mix (if rates drop, interest expense falls faster than interest income due to deposit repricing benefit),

  • Operating leverage (expenses growing slower than revenues),

  • Possibly accretive acquisitions (management has hinted they’d buy another bank if it’s a good fit, which could instantly boost EPS if done at the right price).

Even if we assumed a slightly lower EPS growth, say 12–15%, Bank7 would double EPS in ~5 years. But let’s stick with 15% CAGR for modeling.

5-Year Scenario: If EPS grows from $4.50 now to, say, $9.05 in five years (that’s 15% CAGR), and we assign a 11x multiple then, the stock could be $100 ($62 when discounted back).

Even if the multiple stayed where it is but EPS grows 15%, you’d get 15% stock price appreciation, still great and well above market average expectations. The combo of multiple expansion and earnings growth is powerful.

Why the Market May Re-rate BSVN: A few catalysts could drive P/E upward:

  • Continued earnings beats (they beat in Q2 and Q3 2025) building credibility.

  • More coverage or inclusion in bank indexes as it crosses certain size thresholds (it’s possible a small-cap index fund or bank ETF picks more shares, raising demand).

  • Insider actions like a buyback or special dividend could signal confidence, prompting investors to pay a higher multiple.

  • Simply time. As Bank7 proves it can maintain high ROE across cycles, investors may treat it more like a growth stock than a cyclical bank, thus warranting a higher multiple.

P/B Perspective: At 1.6x, the stock isn’t cheap on assets. However, with ROE ~20%, it’s earning well above its cost of equity, justifying a premium P/B. If ROE stays high, the P/B will likely stay elevated. I don’t see P/B as a limiting factor unless ROE were to collapse. To gauge, if Bank7 trades up to 12x earnings and earns $5 in 2026, that’s $60 stock. Book value by then might be $30 (retaining earnings), so P/B would be 2.0x. Not outrageous for a quality compounder bank.

Valuation Summary: In my view, Bank7 is undervalued by at ~50% to what I think is its fair share value of $62. And over a multi-year horizon, I see potential for the stock to double as earnings compound and the market rewards its consistency. The risk-reward is favorable: at 9x earnings, there’s a margin of safety if earnings slip; but if they grow as expected, upside is substantial.

One more point: takeover possibility. Mergers in banking have slowed, but Bank7 could still play on either side of that equation. It has the balance sheet to buy a smaller bank using stock or cash accretively. Or a larger regional could take interest in Bank7 for its profitability and strong markets. The catch is ownership. With the Haines family controlling nearly half the shares, any deal would need to come with a substantial premium for them to even consider letting go. If a suitor showed up, the offer would likely need to clear 2.2–2.5× book value, maybe higher.

All told, by standard metrics and by considering its growth, BSVN appears undervalued. There is a clear disconnect between Bank7’s exceptional fundamentals and its modest valuation.

Risks and the Bear Case

Risk #1. Interest Rate Risk (NIM Compression)

A rapid decline in interest rates could squeeze Bank7’s NIM. The Federal Reserve has already begun cutting rates (most recently reducing the fed-funds target to 3.75-4.00% in October) and markets expect another cut in December.

Here’s how things look now for Bank7:

  • So far it has managed well despite the initial rate cuts. Management reports that loan yields remain strong (around 7.6% in Q2 2025) and deposit costs have declined faster than expected.

  • Bank7 emphasizes that around 79% of its loans are variable-rate and many have interest-rate floors, while deposit beta (how fast deposit costs rise) has lagged early cuts, creating a cushion.

  • Given this positioning, the margin hasn’t yet collapsed. Management expects only modest margin compression if rates fall further, rather than full normalization to peer levels.

Nevertheless the risk persists:

  • If rates continue to fall further and faster than anticipated, the floor protection on loans can erode over time (Bank7 states 95% of its loans reprice or mature within 5 years).

  • Deposit cost relief may slow if competition for deposits increases (or if the bank needs to raise rates to retain funds).

  • In a scenario where NIM falls from 5% to closer to peer levels (say 3.5-4%), then net interest income could stagnate or decline, hurting earnings. That would make Bank7’s formerly premium returns drop into average-bank territory.

  • While I believe Bank7’s structure and management give it a better buffer than most peers, it is not immune to macro risk. The bear-case is that the recent high margins were cyclical peaks and may revert.

In short: Bank7 has done a good job so far navigating the early cuts. But if the rate-cut cycle accelerates or deposit competition intensifies, the margin cushion could thin and that’s a risk worth keeping front of mind.

Risk #2. Limited Float and Liquidity

With substantial insider ownership and Bank7’s low market cap ($390M), Bank7’s stock isn’t very liquid. In a market downturn, low liquidity can exacerbate price declines as any selling pressure has outsized impact. It also may deter some big institutional investors from buying, keeping valuations lower than peers with more float. This is a minor risk, but for a holder it means possibly higher volatility.

Bear Case Outcome

Let’s envision a bear-case valuation: EPS drops to $3.50 (a ~20% cut from current run-rate) due to narrower margins and higher provisions. Investors get skittish and assign an 8x P/E (typical in a downturn for banks). That yields a stock around $28. This implies about a 30% downside from current levels. Not pleasant, but not catastrophic given the upside potential is double that. Moreover, during such a downturn, Bank7 would still be profitable and likely still paying a dividend, so patient investors could hold through.

To me, the biggest risk to watch is net interest margin pressure in 2024-2025 if the Fed starts cutting aggressively. We’ll want to see how Bank7 manages deposit costs down. The early signs are good (they have strategy with floors, etc.), but the proof will be in the numbers. Also, keeping an eye on loan growth. If it starts to stagnate, that would be a warning sign that the franchise isn’t getting new business as expected.

In summary, the bear case exists mostly under a scenario of macroeconomic strain. Bank7’s own execution has been near-flawless, so the risks are more external (rates, economy) and valuation perception. I’m comforted that even in those cases, Bank7’s financial strength provides a margin of safety as it’s not a highly leveraged or fragile bank.

Other Angles: Long-Term Thesis Support

Beyond the core fundamentals, there are additional angles to why Bank7 makes sense as a long-term investment:

  • “Picks and Shovels” of Local Economy: Think of Bank7 as an indirect play on the heartland economy (energy, agriculture, small business) but in a risk-controlled way. If oil & gas or farming does well, Oklahoma and Kansas thrive and Bank7 benefits from more deposits and loan demand. If those sectors struggle, Bank7 still has enough diversification and loan collateral to weather it (plus much of energy risk was pruned). It’s like owning a slice of the local economic engine, with Bank7 as the banker facilitating commerce. Over decades, local economies tend to grow, and Bank7 can ride that secular growth by sticking to its knitting.

  • Dividends and Potential Increases: Bank7 initiated a dividend a few years ago and has kept increasing it. With a low payout ratio and high profitability, there’s room for continued dividend growth. I expect management will continue raising the dividend. If EPS grows 15% a year, the dividend could similarly grow, potentially doubling in 5 years. A 3% yield on cost five years out (assuming dividend increases) is a nice bonus to the thesis.

  • Inflation Hedge Qualities: Banks aren’t classic inflation hedges, but Bank7 comes close. In inflationary times, it can reprice loans upwards (79% variable loans) and has low fixed-rate assets, so its interest income keeps pace with rising prices. They also have low operating leverage (not a huge branch network to maintain), so expense growth can be managed. Thus, if inflation surprises on upside, Bank7 could actually benefit (as seen in 2022–23).

Verdict: A Big “Buy” on This Small Bank

Bank7 is my stock pick for this month because it checks all the boxes of a standout opportunity:

  • Quality of Business: Excellent. Bank7 is a deep dive into what makes a great bank: high margins, efficient operations, and prudent risk management. Few banks its size have this level of consistent excellence in profitability.

  • Undervaluation: The stock is mispriced in my opinion. At 9 times earnings, the market treats it like an average bank, whereas it’s arguably one of the best banks in terms of fundamentals. A re-rating to even 11x earnings would yield substantial upside, not to mention the growth kicker.

  • Growth Runway: Far from being ex-growth, Bank7 has multiple growth levers from organically expanding in prosperous markets to possibly making smart acquisitions and simply leveraging its high returns by reinvesting earnings. An EPS CAGR of ~15% is ambitious but credible given recent performance.

  • Shareholder-Friendly Management: Insiders are aligned with us, there’s a dividend that’s likely to grow, and capital is handled judiciously. They’ve shown they can both beat the tide of industry challenges and swim strongly with it when conditions are good.

  • Risks Manageable: Downside scenarios, while real, seem contained by the bank’s strong balance sheet and conservative approach. In a tough environment, Bank7 is the kind of bank that survives and even gains relative strength.

At the current price, I see an attractive entry point. We get a well-run business at a value price, but in the banking sector. Over a 1-2 year horizon, I believe Bank7 can deliver 40-50% stock appreciation (through some combination of multiple expansion and earnings growth), plus dividends. Over a longer horizon (3-5 years), it has the potential to double as it continues to compound book value and earnings.
